title: The tired office worker
scene: A 42-year-old presents with several months of fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, and gradual weight gain. No new medications.
vitals: HR 58; BP 124/78; afebrile

questions.prompt: What single diagnosis best explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: Cold intolerance, constipation and bradycardia are a classic cluster for low thyroid hormone activity; other causes of fatigue remain on the differential.
questions.hint: Which endocrine disorder slows basal metabolic activity?

questions.prompt: Which initial laboratory strategy best establishes the suspected diagnosis?
options: TSH followed by free T4 when indicated
questions.explanation: TSH is the usual first test for primary thyroid dysfunction; free T4 characterizes the biochemical pattern.
questions.hint: Which pituitary signal responds to falling thyroid hormone?
questions.probe: How would central hypothyroidism change the expected TSH pattern?
questions.probeAnswer: Free T4 is low, but TSH may be low or inappropriately normal.
questions.update: TSH returns elevated with low free T4.

questions.prompt: Why is the resting heart rate lower than expected?
options: Reduced thyroid hormone lowers chronotropy and metabolic demand
A primary vagal nerve lesion is inevitable
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone promotes cardiac rate, contractility, and tissue metabolic activity; deficiency generally slows the system.
questions.hint: Think about thyroid hormone effects on cardiac gene expression.

questions.prompt: Which long-term treatment is typically indicated for overt primary disease?
options: Oral levothyroxine with follow-up TSH monitoring
questions.explanation: Levothyroxine replaces T4; TSH is rechecked after dose adjustments, with individualized dosing for age and cardiac risk.
questions.hint: Replace the hormone that the thyroid is failing to produce.
questions.probe: Why be more cautious with replacement in coronary artery disease?
questions.probeAnswer: Rapid increases in metabolic demand can precipitate ischemia in susceptible patients.

questions.prompt: What clinically important problem can occur with excessive replacement?
options: Severe neutropenia as the typical effect
questions.explanation: Excess thyroid hormone can cause iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis, including arrhythmias and accelerated bone loss.
questions.hint: Think about too much rather than too little thyroid hormone.

questions.prompt: The patient takes calcium supplements with the morning medication. What counseling matters?
options: Separate calcium from levothyroxine because absorption is reduced
Take calcium at the same time to enhance absorption
questions.explanation: Calcium and iron can impair levothyroxine absorption; consistent administration timing matters.
questions.hint: Consider drug–nutrient interactions in the gut.

stable: Energy improves gradually with hormone replacement and biochemical follow-up.
unstable: The patient misses follow-up and symptoms persist, prompting medication reconciliation and repeat thyroid studies.

title: Thirst after a routine checkup
scene: A 51-year-old reports increased thirst, nocturia, fatigue and slowly worsening blurred vision. A parent has diabetes.
vitals: BMI 33; BP 138/84; no acute distress

questions.prompt: Which condition is most likely?
questions.explanation: Polyuria and polydipsia with metabolic risk factors raise concern for hyperglycemia.
questions.hint: What solute can cause osmotic diuresis?

questions.prompt: Which finding would meet a standard diagnostic criterion in a symptomatic patient?
options: Random plasma glucose at least 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms
Urine glucose alone without plasma confirmation
questions.explanation: Classic symptoms plus random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL can establish diabetes; other thresholds include fasting plasma glucose ≥126 and A1c ≥6.5%, with confirmation rules depending on context.
questions.hint: Recall the diagnostic random glucose threshold.
questions.probe: Why might A1c be unreliable in some patients?
questions.probeAnswer: Altered red-cell turnover or hemoglobin variants can distort A1c.

questions.prompt: What primarily causes the increased urination?
options: Filtered glucose exceeding renal reabsorptive capacity causes osmotic diuresis
The bladder loses its parasympathetic innervation
questions.explanation: When glucosuria occurs, tubular glucose retains water in the lumen and increases urine output.
questions.hint: Follow water movement through the renal tubule.

questions.prompt: For an uncomplicated stable outpatient, what is the best broad initial approach?
options: Lifestyle intervention plus individualized glucose-lowering therapy and cardiovascular risk management
Insulin infusion for every newly diagnosed patient
Antibiotics for presumed urinary infection alone
questions.explanation: Outpatient management addresses glycemia and cardiovascular, renal and weight-related risks; drug selection should reflect comorbidities and shared decisions.
questions.hint: Think beyond a single glucose value.

questions.prompt: Which presentation requires urgent evaluation for a hyperglycemic emergency?
options: Stable fasting glucose mildly above target
questions.explanation: Volume depletion, acidosis or hyperosmolality can cause life-threatening metabolic emergencies.
questions.hint: Which features suggest systemic decompensation?

questions.prompt: Why should kidney and urine albumin screening be part of longitudinal care?
options: Albuminuria and reduced eGFR may signal diabetic kidney disease before symptoms
Albuminuria is only relevant in type 1 diabetes
A normal blood pressure excludes kidney disease
questions.explanation: Early detection of kidney involvement changes risk management and follow-up.
questions.hint: Consider silent microvascular injury.

stable: A personalized treatment and screening plan is established at follow-up.
unstable: The patient becomes dehydrated during an intercurrent illness, requiring evaluation for hyperglycemic crisis.

sources.label: ADA — Standards of Care in Diabetes (2026)

title: Cough that comes and goes
scene: A 24-year-old has intermittent nighttime cough, episodic chest tightness and shortness of breath when running. Symptoms vary week to week.
vitals: SpO₂ 98%; clear lungs between episodes

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis should be high on the differential?
questions.explanation: Variable respiratory symptoms and triggers are characteristic of asthma; objective testing is needed.
questions.hint: Think of variable rather than fixed airflow limitation.

questions.prompt: Which test finding would support the diagnosis?
options: Variable expiratory airflow limitation on spirometry with bronchodilator response
questions.explanation: A variable obstructive pattern with significant bronchodilator reversibility supports asthma, though a normal test between episodes does not exclude it.
questions.hint: Look for reversibility in expiratory flow.
questions.probe: Why might spirometry be normal between episodes?
questions.probeAnswer: Airway narrowing varies over time and with exposures.

questions.prompt: What physiologic process produces episodic expiratory limitation?
options: Airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction increase resistance
Loss of pulmonary surfactant is the primary mechanism
Alveolar fibrosis increases total lung capacity
questions.explanation: Inflamed, hyperresponsive airways narrow from smooth-muscle contraction, edema and mucus.
questions.hint: What happens to a small airway radius?

questions.prompt: What principle characterizes current controller-based therapy for adults with asthma?
options: Use an inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimen rather than SABA-only treatment
Use oral antibiotics for every episode
Long-term oral steroid monotherapy for mild symptoms
questions.explanation: GINA recommends ICS-containing therapy for adults and adolescents rather than treating with SABA alone; exact track and inhaler depend on severity and availability.
questions.hint: What treats inflammation as well as bronchospasm?
questions.probe: What does formoterol contribute to certain reliever regimens?
questions.probeAnswer: Rapid-onset bronchodilation paired with ICS in a combination inhaler.

questions.prompt: Which sign suggests a life-threatening exacerbation?
options: Silent chest with exhaustion and altered consciousness
questions.explanation: Little audible airflow in a severely obstructed, tiring patient is dangerous, not reassuring.
questions.hint: Less wheezing is not always better.

questions.prompt: Why should inhaler technique and adherence be checked before stepping up therapy?
options: Poor delivery or inconsistent use can mimic treatment failure
Inhaler technique cannot affect distal airway exposure
ICS efficacy is independent of airway deposition
questions.explanation: Technique, access and adherence are modifiable contributors to poor control.
questions.hint: Think about how the drug reaches the target.

stable: The patient practices correct inhaler use and receives an action plan.
unstable: Symptoms intensify after a respiratory illness, and the patient needs an urgent severity assessment.

title: Blood pressure that stays high
scene: A 44-year-old has persistently elevated blood pressure despite three antihypertensives, including a diuretic. He reports muscle weakness.
vitals: BP 166/98; K⁺ 3.0 mmol/L

questions.prompt: What secondary cause is particularly concerning?
questions.explanation: Resistant hypertension with unexplained hypokalemia strongly raises suspicion for excess aldosterone, although normal potassium does not exclude it.
questions.hint: What hormone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium loss?

questions.prompt: What screening test best addresses that concern?
options: Plasma aldosterone and renin assessment with their ratio
questions.explanation: An elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio with appropriate aldosterone context prompts further evaluation; medications and potassium can affect interpretation.
questions.hint: Which two hormones should be assessed together?

questions.prompt: Why can this disorder lower serum potassium?
options: Increased distal nephron sodium uptake promotes potassium secretion
Reduced distal sodium delivery always increases potassium secretion
It causes insulin absence and ketoacidosis
questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption and favors potassium and hydrogen ion secretion.
questions.hint: Think about principal cells in the collecting duct.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate next step after suggestive screening?
options: Confirm the diagnosis and evaluate subtype while correcting potassium and reviewing interfering drugs
Proceed to adrenalectomy in every patient
questions.explanation: Definitive workup depends on clinical context and includes confirmation and localization/subtyping when indicated.
questions.hint: Screening does not always establish unilateral disease.

questions.prompt: Which complication is a major reason to treat aldosterone excess?
options: Increased cardiovascular and renal injury beyond blood-pressure effects
Reduced risk of stroke without treatment
questions.explanation: Aldosterone excess is linked with disproportionate cardiac and renal injury.
questions.hint: Think of long-term organ damage.

questions.prompt: Why is adrenal vein sampling sometimes needed before surgery?
options: CT appearance alone may not identify the aldosterone-producing side
It measures the glomerular filtration rate directly
It rules out all adrenal malignancy
It determines the thyroid replacement dose
questions.explanation: Functional lateralization may differ from incidental structural adrenal nodules.
questions.hint: An imaging abnormality is not necessarily the source.

stable: Blood pressure and potassium improve with targeted management.
unstable: Persistent uncontrolled blood pressure prompts assessment of adherence, organ injury and a specialist workup.

title: Abnormal kidney tests
scene: A 60-year-old with long-standing diabetes and hypertension is seen after routine laboratory monitoring.
vitals: BP 148/86; eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m²; urine albumin-creatinine ratio 520 mg/g

questions.prompt: What problem do these findings most strongly suggest?
options: Chronic kidney disease with substantial albuminuria
questions.explanation: Persistently reduced eGFR and high albuminuria support CKD and signify elevated renal and cardiovascular risk.
questions.hint: Consider both filtration and albumin leakage.

questions.prompt: What is needed before labeling a new isolated abnormal result as chronic?
options: Evidence of kidney abnormality persisting at least three months
A repeat result only 24 hours later
questions.explanation: CKD requires abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for ≥3 months.
questions.hint: What is the time component in chronic kidney disease?

questions.prompt: Why does glomerular injury cause albuminuria?
options: Damage to the filtration barrier increases albumin passage
Aldosterone directly converts albumin into creatinine
Protein synthesis by the liver always doubles
Normal podocytes actively secrete large amounts of albumin
questions.explanation: The endothelial–basement membrane–podocyte barrier normally limits albumin filtration.
questions.hint: Think about podocytes and the basement membrane.

questions.prompt: Which management strategy most directly reduces long-term risk in appropriate patients?
options: Optimize BP and glycemia with indicated kidney-protective agents such as RAS blockade and SGLT2 inhibition
Avoid blood-pressure treatment to preserve perfusion
questions.explanation: Renoprotective choices depend on eGFR, albuminuria, potassium, comorbidities and contraindications; avoid nephrotoxins.
questions.hint: Which drug classes protect the kidney beyond lowering sugar?

questions.prompt: What should be monitored after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB?
options: Platelet count as the only measure
questions.explanation: RAS blockade can alter efferent arteriolar tone and increase potassium; assess renal function and potassium after initiation or titration.
questions.hint: Which electrolyte rises when aldosterone signaling falls?

questions.prompt: Why is an elevated urine albumin-creatinine ratio prognostically important even with moderate eGFR reduction?
options: Albuminuria independently predicts renal progression and cardiovascular risk
Albuminuria has no risk significance until dialysis
Albuminuria proves nephrotic syndrome in every patient
questions.explanation: Both eGFR and albuminuria contribute to CKD risk staging.
questions.hint: Do not interpret eGFR alone.

stable: Risk factors are addressed with laboratory monitoring and shared decisions.
unstable: Potassium rises after a medication change, requiring reassessment of therapy and kidney function.

title: Episodes of racing heartbeat
scene: A 71-year-old describes intermittent palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance. An irregularly irregular pulse is detected.
vitals: HR 118 irregular; BP 132/80

questions.prompt: What arrhythmia is most likely?
questions.explanation: An irregularly irregular rhythm without organized atrial P waves is characteristic of atrial fibrillation.
questions.hint: Which common supraventricular rhythm is irregularly irregular?

questions.prompt: What is the best immediate study to characterize the rhythm?
options: Chest CT with contrast as the first rhythm test
questions.explanation: An ECG can confirm rhythm and identify concerning features; ambulatory monitoring may be needed if intermittent and absent during the visit.
questions.hint: What directly records electrical cardiac activity?

questions.prompt: Why does this rhythm increase ischemic stroke risk?
options: Ineffective atrial contraction allows stasis and atrial thrombus formation
It always causes coronary plaque rupture
The ventricles directly form carotid emboli
High cardiac output removes clotting factors
questions.explanation: Stasis, particularly in the left atrial appendage, facilitates thromboembolism.
questions.hint: Think about atrial mechanical function.

questions.prompt: In a stable patient, what broad decisions are central to management?
options: Assess rate or rhythm control and thromboembolic risk
Treat only with aspirin regardless of risk
questions.explanation: Treatment balances symptoms, rhythm strategy, stroke prevention, comorbidity and bleeding risk; unstable patients need urgent stabilization.
questions.hint: Separate symptom control from stroke prevention.

questions.prompt: What clinical finding changes the urgency of management?
options: Hypotension with ischemic chest pain or shock
A stable blood pressure and mild palpitations
questions.explanation: Hemodynamic compromise with tachyarrhythmia may require prompt synchronized cardioversion under appropriate protocols.
questions.hint: Think about hemodynamic stability.

questions.prompt: Why should stroke prevention not be determined solely by whether the patient feels palpitations?
options: Thromboembolic risk depends on clinical risk factors, not symptom awareness
Asymptomatic episodes are never atrial fibrillation
Anticoagulation is only for heart rates over 150
A normal pulse at one visit eliminates prior risk
questions.explanation: Risk assessment remains important in paroxysmal or minimally symptomatic AF.
questions.hint: Symptoms do not equal clot risk.

stable: Rate and stroke-risk plans are individualized after ECG confirmation.
unstable: The patient develops hypotension and chest discomfort during rapid conduction and needs urgent reassessment.

title: Vomiting with rapid breathing
scene: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain and missed insulin doses during a viral illness.
vitals: HR 124; RR 30; glucose 490 mg/dL; bicarbonate 10 mmol/L; β-hydroxybutyrate high

questions.prompt: Which metabolic emergency best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Insulin deficiency with ketonemia and metabolic acidosis supports DKA.
questions.hint: Combine hyperglycemia, ketones and low bicarbonate.

questions.prompt: Which blood-gas pattern is expected?
questions.explanation: Ketoacids lower bicarbonate; compensatory hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂.
questions.hint: What should happen to pH and carbon dioxide?

questions.prompt: Why does serum potassium sometimes look normal or high despite total-body potassium depletion?
options: Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium extracellularly while urinary losses deplete stores
Kidneys retain all potassium during osmotic diuresis
All potassium is generated by ketones
Insulin deficiency moves potassium into cells
questions.explanation: Serum potassium can mask severe total-body deficit; insulin therapy can rapidly lower serum potassium.
questions.hint: Differentiate serum concentration from total-body stores.
questions.probe: Why is potassium checked before insulin?
questions.probeAnswer: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and may provoke dangerous hypokalemia.

questions.prompt: What is the best general treatment framework?
options: IV fluids, insulin, electrolyte management and treatment of the trigger
Withhold all fluids until ketones disappear
questions.explanation: Guideline-directed DKA management requires careful fluid resuscitation, insulin and electrolyte monitoring, tailored to severity and patient factors.
questions.hint: Correct circulation and insulin deficiency together.

questions.prompt: What is an immediate safety concern if potassium is markedly low before insulin begins?
questions.explanation: Severe hypokalemia should be corrected before insulin according to the treatment pathway; monitor ECG and electrolytes.
questions.hint: What happens when insulin drives K⁺ into cells?

questions.prompt: Why is an appropriate subcutaneous insulin bridge needed when ending IV insulin?
options: Abrupt discontinuation can reopen the insulin gap and cause rebound ketoacidosis
IV insulin has a week-long duration
questions.explanation: Basal coverage should overlap before stopping the infusion to prevent recurrent insulin deficiency.
questions.hint: Consider insulin pharmacokinetics during transition.

stable: The anion gap resolves, electrolytes stabilize and a safe insulin transition is arranged.
unstable: Potassium falls during treatment, prompting ECG monitoring and electrolyte replacement before further insulin adjustment.

sources.label: ADA Standards of Care 2025 — hospital care

title: Pressure in the chest
scene: A 63-year-old develops 45 minutes of substernal pressure radiating to the left arm with nausea and sweating.
vitals: BP 146/88; HR 104; ECG with ST elevation in II, III and aVF

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis requires immediate action?
options: Acute pericarditis with diffuse ST elevation
questions.explanation: Contiguous inferior ST elevation with ischemic symptoms indicates STEMI until proven otherwise.
questions.hint: Which ECG territory corresponds to II, III and aVF?

questions.prompt: What is the most time-critical system-level intervention?
options: Wait for serial troponins before acting
questions.explanation: Rapid reperfusion is central to acute STEMI care; do not delay for biomarker confirmation.
questions.hint: Time is myocardium.
questions.probe: Which coronary artery commonly supplies the inferior wall?
questions.probeAnswer: Usually the right coronary artery, though dominance varies.

questions.prompt: How does coronary artery occlusion cause contractile failure?
options: Ischemia depletes ATP and disrupts calcium handling in cardiomyocytes
Myocytes produce unlimited ATP without oxygen
Coronary occlusion instantly increases oxidative phosphorylation
Cardiac actin is unaffected by energy availability
questions.explanation: Oxygen deprivation compromises ATP-dependent ion handling and contraction, progressing to necrosis if not relieved.
questions.hint: What fuels ion pumps and cross-bridge cycling?

questions.prompt: What general medication strategy accompanies reperfusion when appropriate?
options: Antiplatelet therapy and other guideline-directed ACS medication with bleeding and contraindication assessment
Routine thrombolysis after successful PCI for everyone
Avoid all antithrombotics regardless of circumstance
questions.explanation: ACS treatment generally includes antiplatelet treatment and secondary prevention, tailored to bleeding risk and revascularization strategy.
questions.hint: Think about platelet-rich coronary thrombus.

questions.prompt: After an inferior infarct, which associated conduction problem warrants monitoring?
options: Mandatory long QT syndrome in every patient
questions.explanation: The AV nodal blood supply is often linked to the RCA and can be affected in inferior infarction.
questions.hint: Consider the artery supplying the AV node.

questions.prompt: Why should nitrates be used cautiously when right ventricular infarction is suspected?
options: Preload reduction may cause profound hypotension
questions.explanation: Right ventricular infarction can be preload sensitive; assess hemodynamics and contraindications before nitrates.
questions.hint: Which ventricle may depend critically on venous return?

stable: The patient receives rapid reperfusion and monitoring for conduction disturbances.
unstable: Bradycardia and hypotension develop, requiring assessment for right ventricular involvement and conduction block.

title: Short of breath at night
scene: A 74-year-old with hypertension and prior myocardial infarction has progressive orthopnea, weight gain and bilateral leg swelling.
vitals: SpO₂ 88%; HR 110; JVP elevated; bilateral crackles

questions.prompt: What syndrome is most likely responsible?
options: Acute decompensated heart failure with congestion
Pulmonary embolism as the only diagnosis
questions.explanation: Orthopnea, jugular venous distention, crackles and edema strongly suggest elevated cardiac filling pressures and congestion.
questions.hint: What unifies lung fluid and leg edema?

questions.prompt: Which initial investigation combination is particularly useful?
options: ECG, chest imaging, natriuretic peptides and renal/electrolyte assessment
questions.explanation: Cardiac, pulmonary and renal evaluation helps identify congestion, myocardial injury and precipitants.
questions.hint: What tests assess both congestion and its cause?

questions.prompt: Why does left-sided filling pressure produce pulmonary crackles?
options: Elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure drives fluid into interstitium and alveoli
Low pulmonary venous pressure forces edema
Reduced capillary permeability always creates pulmonary edema
Airway smooth-muscle contraction is the only mechanism
questions.explanation: Raised pulmonary venous hydrostatic pressure increases transudation into lung interstitium.
questions.hint: Recall Starling forces in pulmonary capillaries.

questions.prompt: In a congested patient without shock, which treatment direction is typical?
options: Oxygenation support as needed and IV loop diuresis while evaluating causes
Routine large crystalloid boluses regardless of volume status
Broad-spectrum antibiotics as the sole intervention
questions.explanation: Decongestion and monitoring of renal function and electrolytes are central; address ischemia, arrhythmia and other triggers.
questions.hint: Treat volume overload, not just dyspnea.

questions.prompt: Which diuretic-related complication should be monitored?
options: Neutropenia as the usual dose-limiting issue
questions.explanation: Loop diuretics alter electrolyte excretion and volume status, requiring follow-up labs and examination.
questions.hint: Where do loop diuretics act in the nephron?

questions.prompt: Why can a normal ejection fraction still coexist with heart failure symptoms?
options: Impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures can cause HFpEF
Normal EF excludes all cardiac dysfunction
Cardiac output always doubles when EF is normal
Diastolic function has no influence on venous pressures
questions.explanation: Ejection fraction measures relative systolic emptying and does not directly establish normal filling pressures.
questions.hint: Separate systolic emptying from diastolic compliance.

stable: Oxygenation and congestion improve with careful diuresis.
unstable: Renal function and blood pressure deteriorate after treatment, prompting reassessment of perfusion and volume status.

title: The wheezing infant
scene: A 5-month-old has rhinorrhea and cough followed by poor feeding and increased work of breathing. Several daycare contacts are ill.
vitals: RR 54; SpO₂ 93%; diffuse crackles and wheeze; mild retractions

questions.prompt: What clinical syndrome best fits this presentation?
options: Foreign body aspiration with sudden onset
questions.explanation: A viral upper respiratory prodrome followed by diffuse lower-airway signs in an infant is characteristic of bronchiolitis.
questions.hint: Age, prodrome and diffuse findings matter.

questions.prompt: In an otherwise typical, stable presentation, what is the usual diagnostic approach?
options: Clinical diagnosis with assessment of feeding, oxygenation and work of breathing
Routine CT chest for all infants
Routine bacterial blood cultures for every child
Routine chest radiography to confirm all cases
questions.explanation: Typical bronchiolitis is diagnosed clinically; imaging and testing are reserved for selected atypical or complicated situations.
questions.hint: Which bedside features predict the need for support?

questions.prompt: Why do infants develop substantial respiratory distress from small airway swelling?
options: Small baseline bronchiolar radius makes resistance rise steeply with narrowing
Infant airways are immune to mucus plugging
Alveolar oxygen always rises with edema
questions.explanation: Resistance increases dramatically as small airway radius decreases, with mucus and edema adding obstruction.
questions.hint: Recall the inverse-fourth-power relationship to radius.

questions.prompt: What is the mainstay of management?
options: Supportive hydration, suction as appropriate and respiratory support based on severity
Routine systemic steroids for all cases
Universal bronchodilator therapy regardless of response
questions.explanation: Supportive care targets oxygenation, hydration and work of breathing; routine medications are usually not beneficial in classic bronchiolitis.
questions.hint: What problem must be supported while infection resolves?

questions.prompt: Which finding makes admission or escalation more concerning?
options: Apnea, exhaustion or inability to maintain hydration
questions.explanation: Apnea, significant work of breathing, poor oral intake and hypoxemia raise the need for monitoring and respiratory support.
questions.hint: Which symptoms reflect failure to maintain ventilation or intake?

questions.prompt: Why may wheezing be an unreliable measure of overall severity?
options: A tiring infant with very poor air movement may wheeze less
Loud wheezing always indicates impending respiratory arrest
Noisy breathing proves normal gas exchange
questions.explanation: Clinical trajectory, perfusion, fatigue and oxygenation matter more than sound intensity alone.
questions.hint: Less airflow can mean less noise.

stable: Feeding and respiratory effort improve with supportive care and monitoring.
unstable: Oral intake drops and apnea is reported, requiring urgent reassessment of respiratory support.

title: Noisy breathing at bedtime
scene: A 2-year-old wakes with a harsh cough and noisy breathing after two days of congestion. The voice sounds hoarse.
vitals: T 38.1°C; inspiratory stridor when upset; no drooling

questions.prompt: What diagnosis most closely fits?
questions.explanation: Barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor with a viral prodrome suggest laryngotracheitis.
questions.hint: Where is the obstruction: upper or lower airway?

questions.prompt: Which feature is most helpful for judging immediate severity?
options: Stridor at rest together with work of breathing and mental status
questions.explanation: Stridor at rest, retractions, cyanosis, fatigue and distress inform severity more than a cough alone.
questions.hint: Evaluate breathing at rest.

questions.prompt: Why does swelling below the vocal cords cause inspiratory noise?
options: Subglottic airway narrowing generates turbulent upper-airway flow
Alveolar fluid directly creates laryngeal stridor
questions.explanation: Subglottic mucosal edema narrows the relatively small pediatric airway and produces stridor.
questions.hint: Think anatomically about the cricoid region.

questions.prompt: Which medication is useful across most severities of classic croup?
options: A systemic corticosteroid such as dexamethasone
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone reduces airway inflammation; nebulized epinephrine may be added for moderate or severe symptoms with observation for recurrence.
questions.hint: Which drug reduces upper-airway inflammation?
questions.probe: What additional intervention may be used in more severe croup?
questions.probeAnswer: Nebulized epinephrine alongside steroid and close reassessment.

questions.prompt: Which change should trigger concern for an alternative dangerous diagnosis?
options: Drooling, toxic appearance and inability to handle secretions
questions.explanation: Drooling with a toxic child suggests another upper-airway emergency such as epiglottitis or deep neck infection.
questions.hint: What suggests an inability to protect the airway?

questions.prompt: Why is observation required after nebulized epinephrine in more severe disease?
options: Its vasoconstrictive benefit is temporary and symptoms can recur
Epinephrine permanently cures the viral infection
The drug takes several days to act
questions.explanation: Repeat assessment is important as the short-lived reduction in edema wears off.
questions.hint: How long does a local adrenergic effect persist?

stable: Noisy breathing settles after appropriate therapy and observation.
unstable: Stridor becomes persistent at rest with increasing fatigue, requiring escalation.

title: A child with a painful limp
scene: A 7-year-old has fever and acute refusal to bear weight on the right leg. Hip movement is markedly painful.
vitals: T 39.2°C; HR 128; limited passive hip range of motion

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
questions.explanation: Fever, inability to bear weight and severe pain with passive joint motion raise concern for septic arthritis, a joint-threatening emergency.
questions.hint: Think about an infected joint.

questions.prompt: Which action best helps confirm the diagnosis without delaying urgent care?
options: Urgent orthopedic assessment with joint aspiration for synovial analysis and culture
Routine outpatient MRI several months later
Repeat gait assessment in six weeks without labs
questions.explanation: Synovial fluid assessment and specialist input guide diagnosis and drainage; do not delay emergency care in an unstable child.
questions.hint: What tissue must be sampled when infection is inside a joint?

questions.prompt: Why can infection rapidly damage articular cartilage?
options: Inflammatory mediators and increased joint pressure impair cartilage and perfusion
Cartilage has a rich direct arterial supply resistant to pressure
Bacteria only affect the skin surface
Synovial inflammation always increases cartilage nutrition
questions.explanation: Enzymes, cytokines and increased intra-articular pressure threaten the cartilage and femoral head.
questions.hint: Consider both inflammatory destruction and pressure effects.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate broad treatment strategy?
options: Prompt drainage/source control and empiric IV antibiotics tailored to cultures
No antibiotics if the child is febrile
questions.explanation: Urgent surgical or procedural management plus antibiotics protects the joint; sampling usually precedes antibiotics when clinically safe.
questions.hint: Think infection management and joint preservation.

questions.prompt: What major long-term complication is most concerning with delayed care?
options: Permanent joint destruction or growth disturbance
Improved hip range of motion permanently
questions.explanation: Delayed treatment can cause cartilage injury, avascular injury and functional impairment.
questions.hint: Which structures can be permanently damaged?

questions.prompt: Why is a normal plain radiograph insufficient to exclude early disease?
options: Early synovial infection may not produce radiographic osseous changes
Normal films prove no infection anywhere
X-rays are more sensitive than aspiration for synovial organisms
questions.explanation: Radiographs can assess fracture and other causes but early septic arthritis often lacks definitive osseous changes.
questions.hint: What tissue is directly infected first?

stable: The joint is rapidly evaluated and treated, reducing long-term damage risk.
unstable: Pain and systemic illness worsen, increasing concern for bacteremia and joint injury.

title: Pain moving across the abdomen
scene: A 19-year-old has abdominal pain beginning near the umbilicus and later localizing to the right lower quadrant, with anorexia and nausea.
vitals: T 38.0°C; HR 102; focal RLQ tenderness

questions.prompt: What diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pain migrating from visceral periumbilical to localized RLQ pain with anorexia supports appendicitis.
questions.hint: Where does the pain localize after parietal irritation?

questions.prompt: In a nonpregnant adult when imaging is needed, which modality is commonly preferred?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with appropriate protocol
questions.explanation: CT has high diagnostic accuracy in adults; ultrasound or MRI may be preferred depending on age, pregnancy and context.
questions.hint: Which modality visualizes appendiceal inflammation in adults?

questions.prompt: Why does early pain begin centrally before localizing?
options: Visceral afferent pain precedes somatic parietal peritoneal irritation
Pain always follows the right phrenic nerve
questions.explanation: Visceral midgut afferents produce poorly localized periumbilical pain; parietal inflammation generates sharper localized pain.
questions.hint: Contrast visceral and somatic sensory innervation.

questions.prompt: What management decision follows confirmed uncomplicated appendicitis?
options: Discuss appendectomy versus selected nonoperative antibiotics using patient-specific risks
questions.explanation: Appendectomy is definitive; selected patients with uncomplicated disease may consider antibiotic management after counseling about recurrence and failure.
questions.hint: Management is not identical for all confirmed cases.

questions.prompt: Which new finding suggests perforation or generalized peritonitis?
options: Diffuse rigidity with worsening systemic toxicity
Improved appetite and normal vital signs
questions.explanation: Diffuse peritoneal signs and systemic deterioration suggest progression and require urgent reassessment.
questions.hint: Think beyond localized RLQ tenderness.

questions.prompt: Why does an appendicolith matter during decisions about antibiotics alone?
options: It is associated with higher risk of nonoperative treatment failure or complications
It guarantees there is no perforation
It is a normal finding in every patient
questions.explanation: An appendicolith can obstruct the lumen and may alter suitability for nonoperative management.
questions.hint: What could maintain appendiceal obstruction?

stable: A management strategy is selected with monitoring and return precautions.
unstable: Worsening diffuse tenderness raises concern for perforation and source-control urgency.

sources.label: SAGES — Diagnosis and Treatment of Appendicitis Guideline

title: Pain after a heavy meal
scene: A 45-year-old has persistent right upper quadrant pain, fever and nausea beginning after dinner. Deep inspiration during RUQ palpation worsens pain.
vitals: T 38.5°C; HR 106; RUQ tenderness

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Persistent RUQ pain, fever and a Murphy sign are consistent with gallbladder inflammation.

questions.prompt: Which initial imaging study is commonly preferred?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound can demonstrate stones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid and sonographic Murphy sign.
questions.hint: What modality evaluates gallstones well?

questions.prompt: How can an impacted cystic duct stone produce the symptoms?
options: Obstruction causes gallbladder distention, inflammation and potentially secondary infection
It releases insulin from the pancreas
questions.explanation: Persistent cystic duct obstruction promotes luminal pressure and inflammatory injury.
questions.hint: Trace bile drainage out of the gallbladder.

questions.prompt: What is a typical definitive strategy in an operative candidate?
options: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy with supportive care and antibiotics when indicated
Routine observation alone in all septic patients
questions.explanation: Early cholecystectomy treats the source; timing and alternatives depend on severity and surgical risk.

questions.prompt: Which presentation raises concern for concomitant ascending cholangitis?
options: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain with systemic illness
questions.explanation: Charcot triad suggests cholangitis due to biliary obstruction and infection, potentially requiring urgent biliary drainage.

questions.prompt: Why must the critical view of safety be established during cholecystectomy?
options: To reduce misidentification and bile duct injury
To increase bile duct clipping speed
questions.explanation: Clear identification of cystic duct and artery before division reduces serious biliary injuries.

unstable: Jaundice and hypotension emerge, prompting assessment for biliary obstruction and sepsis.

title: Vomiting and bloating
scene: A 58-year-old with prior abdominal surgery has crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and no flatus.

questions.prompt: What study best characterizes the level and possible complications in many adults?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast when appropriate
questions.explanation: CT can localize obstruction and look for a transition point, ischemia or closed-loop obstruction.
questions.hint: What imaging can identify a transition point?

questions.prompt: Why does bowel distension worsen proximal to an obstruction?
options: Fluid and gas accumulate when forward transit is impaired
The kidney secretes gas into the lumen
Peristalsis stops permanently in every early obstruction
questions.explanation: Swallowed air, secretions and fluid accumulate above the obstructed segment, leading to distension and third spacing.

options: IV fluids, bowel rest, decompression when indicated and close serial assessment
Immediate oral feeding challenge in every patient
questions.explanation: Selected uncomplicated adhesive obstructions can be managed conservatively with careful monitoring; surgery is needed for red flags or failure.

Improving pain and resumption of flatus
questions.explanation: Strangulation, perforation or ischemia requires prompt surgical attention.

Lactate identifies the exact obstruction site

unstable: Pain becomes constant with guarding, raising concern for strangulation or ischemia.

title: Pain after a leg injury

questions.prompt: What limb-threatening complication must be considered?
questions.explanation: Disproportionate progressive pain and pain with passive stretch after a fracture are concerning for elevated compartment pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate next step when suspicion is high?
options: Urgent surgical evaluation and remove external constriction while preparing definitive care
Discharge because distal pulses are present
questions.explanation: Acute compartment syndrome is a time-sensitive surgical emergency; pulses do not exclude it.
questions.hint: Do not wait for late signs.

questions.prompt: Why is tissue injury time dependent?
options: Elevated intracompartmental pressure impairs microvascular perfusion
The fracture instantly blocks all systemic blood flow
Muscle metabolism ceases at normal pressure
questions.explanation: Perfusion pressure across capillaries falls as compartment pressure rises, causing ischemia and necrosis.
questions.hint: Compare capillary pressure with surrounding tissue pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the definitive treatment for established acute compartment syndrome?
questions.explanation: Fasciotomy decompresses the affected fascial compartments and preserves perfusion; urgency is critical.
questions.hint: A tight fascial envelope must be released.

questions.prompt: What can occur after delayed recognition?
options: Volkmann-type ischemic contracture, neuropathy or muscle necrosis
questions.explanation: Irreversible nerve and muscle injury may cause chronic functional loss and systemic rhabdomyolysis complications.
questions.hint: Think irreversible muscle and nerve ischemia.

questions.prompt: Why is a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse falsely reassuring?
options: Macrovascular flow may persist while microvascular perfusion is critically reduced
A normal pulse proves zero swelling
Pulses always disappear before nerve injury
questions.explanation: Compartment syndrome can impair tissue perfusion before large-vessel occlusion or pulse loss.
questions.hint: Distinguish large-vessel flow from capillary flow.

stable: Rapid evaluation and decompression protect muscle and nerve viability.
unstable: Neurologic deficits appear after worsening pressure, raising concern for permanent injury.

title: Flank pain with fever
scene: A 49-year-old has severe colicky left flank pain radiating toward the groin, chills and vomiting.
vitals: T 39.1°C; HR 120; BP 96/58; left costovertebral tenderness

questions.prompt: What dangerous combination should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Obstruction plus fever, tachycardia and hypotension threatens urosepsis and kidney function.
questions.hint: When is a kidney stone more than just a pain problem?

questions.prompt: Which workup is most useful while beginning resuscitation?
options: Urine and blood cultures, renal assessment and prompt imaging for obstruction
Only a pregnancy test in every adult male
questions.explanation: Evaluate sepsis, renal function and the location of obstruction without delaying initial antibiotics and stabilization.
questions.hint: Identify both infection and obstruction.

questions.prompt: Why can antibiotics alone be inadequate?
options: Obstructed infected urine requires drainage for effective source control
Antibiotics are never excreted by kidneys
Fever prevents any drug from circulating
questions.explanation: Persistent obstructed infected urine is a source-control emergency.
questions.hint: Where is the infected fluid trapped?

questions.prompt: What management is time critical?
options: Broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent urinary drainage by stent or nephrostomy
Elective stone observation for several weeks
Treat with analgesics alone and discharge
questions.explanation: Infected obstruction generally requires resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent decompression; definitive stone removal usually follows infection control.
questions.hint: Drain the collecting system, not merely treat pain.

questions.prompt: What complication is most concerning if treatment is delayed?
options: Septic shock and acute kidney injury
questions.explanation: Ongoing infection behind an obstruction can progress to bacteremia, shock and organ injury.
questions.hint: Consider systemic infection and renal consequences.

questions.prompt: Why is definitive stone fragmentation usually deferred during active sepsis?
options: Manipulation can worsen infection and urgent priority is drainage and stabilization
Definitive stone treatment is never possible
Stents are a permanent cure for all stones
Shock improves with any instrumentation regardless of purpose
questions.explanation: Initial source control and hemodynamic stabilization come before elective definitive stone treatment.
questions.hint: Separate emergency decompression from definitive therapy.

stable: The system is decompressed and the patient receives targeted infection treatment.
unstable: Blood pressure worsens with escalating sepsis physiology, requiring critical care and urgent drainage.

title: Sudden scrotal pain
scene: A 16-year-old presents with abrupt severe right testicular pain, nausea and vomiting after sports.
vitals: High-riding tender testis; absent cremasteric reflex on affected side

questions.prompt: What diagnosis must be managed without delay?
questions.explanation: Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain with abnormal lie and absent reflex strongly suggests torsion.
questions.hint: Which condition threatens testicular blood flow?

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate next action in a classic high-suspicion presentation?
options: Immediate urologic consultation for surgical exploration without delaying for imaging
questions.explanation: High clinical suspicion warrants urgent exploration; ultrasound is helpful when uncertain but must not delay time-critical care.
questions.hint: Salvage depends on time.

questions.prompt: Which vascular process causes ischemia in torsion?
options: Twisting of the spermatic cord obstructs venous return and then arterial inflow
The appendix compresses the renal artery
Venous valves form a clot in the IVC
An increase in scrotal skin blood flow causes necrosis
questions.explanation: Spermatic cord rotation raises venous and eventually arterial resistance, causing ischemic injury.
questions.hint: What vessels run within the spermatic cord?

questions.prompt: What is definitive management?
options: Prompt detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy when the testis is viable
Needle drainage of the tunica vaginalis
questions.explanation: Operative detorsion and fixation address the torsed side and protect the other side; nonviable tissue may require orchiectomy.
questions.hint: What prevents recurrence?

questions.prompt: What can result from significant treatment delay?
options: Testicular infarction and loss of fertility potential
Guaranteed spontaneous resolution with no tissue damage
questions.explanation: Prolonged ischemia can cause testicular atrophy or necrosis and future fertility consequences.
questions.hint: Ischemic time determines viability.

questions.prompt: Why should analgesia not be used as a diagnostic trial before urgent consultation?
options: Pain improvement does not reliably exclude ongoing vascular compromise
Torsion always remains maximally painful until surgery
Analgesics irreversibly obscure all physical findings
Pain control is never appropriate in an emergency
questions.explanation: Provide analgesia, but do not delay evaluation or interpret temporary relief as exclusion of torsion.
questions.hint: Clinical urgency is not determined by pain score alone.

stable: Rapid surgical management restores blood flow and protects viability where possible.
unstable: Prolonged ischemia threatens the testis and adds urgency to exploration.

title: Headache late in pregnancy
scene: A 30-year-old at 34 weeks of gestation has a severe persistent headache, right upper quadrant pain and new swelling.
vitals: BP 174/112 on repeat; platelets 88,000/µL; AST elevated

questions.prompt: What diagnosis requires urgent stabilization?
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension and end-organ findings after 20 weeks support preeclampsia with severe features.
questions.hint: Which hypertensive pregnancy syndrome causes multisystem injury?

questions.prompt: Which laboratory panel best assesses end-organ involvement?
options: Platelet count, liver enzymes and serum creatinine with protein evaluation as appropriate
questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and renal dysfunction indicate severity; proteinuria is not mandatory when severe features are present.
questions.hint: Check platelets, liver and kidney.

questions.prompt: What mechanism contributes to systemic endothelial dysfunction?
options: Abnormal placentation and placental signaling disrupt maternal vascular function
Excess fetal insulin directly causes every symptom
questions.explanation: Placental malperfusion and antiangiogenic signaling contribute to widespread endothelial injury and vasoconstriction.
questions.hint: Think placental vascular biology.

questions.prompt: Which immediate priorities are most appropriate?
options: Control severe blood pressure, prevent seizures with magnesium sulfate and plan delivery after stabilization
Observe severe pressures at home without assessment
Continue pregnancy regardless of maternal instability
questions.explanation: Maternal stabilization and timely delivery planning are central; timing depends on gestation, stability and fetal status.
questions.hint: What prevents seizures, and what resolves the placental driver?
questions.probe: Why is delivery considered definitive management?
questions.probeAnswer: Removing the placenta ends the ongoing placental contribution, although postpartum disease may persist.

questions.prompt: What is an important magnesium sulfate toxicity warning sign?
options: Loss of deep tendon reflexes with respiratory depression
Increased patellar reflexes alone after adequate dosing
questions.explanation: Magnesium toxicity can suppress reflexes and respiration; monitor clinical status and renal function.
questions.hint: Magnesium depresses neuromuscular excitability.

questions.prompt: Why can a patient remain at risk after delivery?
options: Preeclampsia and seizures can occur or worsen postpartum
The placental removal instantly normalizes all endothelial function
There is zero postpartum stroke risk
Antihypertensives must always stop at delivery
questions.explanation: Postpartum surveillance remains essential because severe hypertension and eclampsia can persist or present after birth.
questions.hint: Does disease physiology resolve at the moment of delivery?

stable: Maternal blood pressure stabilizes as delivery planning and postpartum monitoring continue.
unstable: Neurologic symptoms worsen, prompting immediate evaluation for eclampsia and other complications.

title: Pain in early pregnancy
scene: A 27-year-old presents with 7 weeks of amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain and spotting. A pregnancy test is positive.
vitals: HR 112; BP 104/68; moderate unilateral tenderness

questions.prompt: Which dangerous diagnosis should be considered first?
questions.explanation: Pain and bleeding with a positive pregnancy test require evaluation for pregnancy of unknown location and ectopic implantation.
questions.hint: Where could a pregnancy implant outside the uterine cavity?

questions.prompt: Which assessment is central to determining location?
options: Transvaginal ultrasonography with quantitative serial hCG interpreted in context
Pap smear as the primary localization test
questions.explanation: Ultrasound and hCG trends help assess pregnancy location; a single hCG level cannot definitively locate or exclude ectopic pregnancy.
questions.hint: Use imaging and trend, not one number.

questions.prompt: Why can rupture cause rapid hemodynamic collapse?
options: Tubal implantation can erode vessels and produce intraperitoneal hemorrhage
Embryonic hormones directly stop all cardiac conduction
Cervical dilation always causes arterial bleeding
A normal uterine pregnancy requires rupture
questions.explanation: The fallopian tube cannot accommodate placental invasion indefinitely; rupture may cause major internal bleeding.
questions.hint: Consider location and local vascular supply.

questions.prompt: What is the priority if the patient develops peritoneal signs and shock?
options: Immediate resuscitation and urgent operative management
questions.explanation: Suspected ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a surgical emergency requiring rapid resuscitation and intervention.
questions.hint: Hemodynamic instability changes the pathway.

questions.prompt: What complication requires explicit counseling when managing stable selected cases medically?
options: Rupture remains possible and urgent return precautions are necessary
questions.explanation: Medical management requires selection criteria, follow-up hCG and recognition of rupture symptoms.
questions.hint: Does medical therapy immediately eliminate rupture risk?

questions.prompt: Why is Rh status considered during management?
options: RhD-negative patients may need anti-D prophylaxis according to current protocols
Rh status determines the ectopic implantation site
questions.explanation: Anti-D decisions depend on Rh status, gestational age, management and local guidance.
questions.hint: Consider maternal sensitization risk.

stable: The pregnancy is localized and the patient receives appropriate definitive or monitored care.
unstable: The patient becomes hypotensive with shoulder pain, raising concern for intraperitoneal bleeding.

title: Bleeding after childbirth
scene: A 32-year-old develops heavy vaginal bleeding shortly after a vaginal delivery. The placenta has delivered.
vitals: HR 132; BP 88/52; uterus feels boggy on palpation

questions.prompt: What is the most likely immediate cause?
options: Placenta previa as a new postpartum diagnosis
questions.explanation: A boggy, poorly contracted uterus with heavy postpartum bleeding suggests uterine atony.
questions.hint: Which of the four Ts relates to tone?

questions.prompt: What initial evaluation should occur simultaneously with resuscitation?
options: Assess uterine tone, quantify bleeding and evaluate the four Ts
Wait for hemoglobin before addressing visible hemorrhage
Delay IV access until bleeding stops
questions.explanation: Tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin are the four major categories of postpartum hemorrhage, while resuscitation proceeds.
questions.hint: What are the four Ts?

questions.prompt: Why does uterine contraction normally limit bleeding after delivery?
options: Myometrial fibers compress vessels at the placental bed
Uterine vessels have no blood pressure after delivery
Placental trophoblast closes all arteries instantly
questions.explanation: Myometrial contraction acts as living ligatures around uterine vessels.
questions.hint: The uterus must compress the placental bed.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate early treatment package?
options: Call for help, uterine massage, uterotonics, resuscitation and early tranexamic acid when indicated
Give anticoagulation as the only therapy
Send the patient home for rest
questions.explanation: PPH management is simultaneous and protocolized, with uterotonics, hemostatic measures, transfusion as needed and escalation for ongoing hemorrhage.
questions.hint: Act on both the uterus and circulating volume.

questions.prompt: Which complication is particularly concerning with ongoing major blood loss?
questions.explanation: Severe hemorrhage can cause hypoperfusion and dilutional or consumptive coagulopathy.
questions.hint: Think about perfusion and clotting factor depletion.

questions.prompt: If the uterus is now firm but bleeding persists, what is the most useful next conceptual step?
options: Evaluate retained tissue, genital tract trauma and coagulation causes
Assume atony remains the only mechanism
Exclude laceration because delivery was vaginal
questions.explanation: Ongoing bleeding despite good tone requires searching for other causes using the four Ts.
questions.hint: A firm fundus shifts the differential.

stable: Bleeding slows with coordinated treatment and the patient receives continued monitoring.
unstable: Bleeding continues despite first-line measures, triggering escalation and a massive hemorrhage protocol.

title: Losing interest in everything
scene: A 29-year-old describes five weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, poor concentration, insomnia and appetite change with impaired function.
vitals: Normal vital signs; no intoxicants reported

questions.prompt: What syndrome is most strongly suggested?
options: Panic attack as the only condition
questions.explanation: At least two weeks of mood or anhedonia symptoms plus associated neurovegetative and cognitive changes raise concern for a major depressive episode.
questions.hint: Consider duration, symptoms and functional impact.

questions.prompt: Which question is essential to ask directly during the initial assessment?
options: Whether the patient has thoughts of suicide, intent or a plan
Only whether they prefer morning appointments
Whether they can name all medications they have ever taken
questions.explanation: Direct, nonjudgmental suicide-risk assessment is a safety priority and does not implant suicidal thoughts.
questions.hint: What immediate risk must never be assumed absent?

questions.prompt: What broad neurobiologic explanation is most accurate?
options: Mood disorders involve distributed neural circuits and multiple neurochemical and psychosocial processes
Depression is always proven by one low serotonin blood test
A single hippocampal lesion causes every episode
questions.explanation: Depression reflects complex circuit, neuroendocrine, inflammatory and contextual contributors; simplistic single-neurotransmitter explanations are insufficient.
questions.hint: Avoid one-neurotransmitter reductionism.

questions.prompt: Which first-line treatment approach is reasonable after individualized assessment?
options: Evidence-based psychotherapy and/or an antidepressant with shared decisions and safety follow-up
Benzodiazepines alone as definitive long-term therapy
Immediate antipsychotic monotherapy for all patients
No follow-up is needed after diagnosis
questions.explanation: Treatment depends on severity, preferences, prior response, comorbidity and safety; monitor response and side effects.
questions.hint: Think evidence-based psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy.

questions.prompt: What history is especially important before prescribing antidepressant monotherapy?
options: Prior mania or hypomania suggesting bipolar disorder
A preference for a particular pharmacy only
questions.explanation: Antidepressant monotherapy may be inappropriate in bipolar disorder and can precipitate switching in some patients.
questions.hint: Could there have been episodes of elevated mood and reduced sleep?

questions.prompt: Why must an early follow-up include renewed safety assessment?
options: Suicidality and clinical status can change while treatment response develops
Treatment cures all symptoms after the first dose
Every patient becomes safe once a prescription is written
questions.explanation: Risk assessment and monitoring remain important early in treatment, especially after changes in symptoms or medications.
questions.hint: Clinical trajectory matters more than a single visit.

stable: A shared treatment and safety plan is started with active follow-up.
unstable: The patient reveals active suicidal intent, prompting urgent safety evaluation and higher level of care.

title: Sleepless and unstoppable

questions.prompt: Which syndrome is most consistent with the presentation?
options: Normal response to a successful week
questions.explanation: Elevated or irritable mood with increased energy, decreased need for sleep and major impairment suggests mania.

questions.prompt: What assessment is essential before determining level of care?
options: Risk of harm, psychosis, substance use and ability to care for self
An IQ test as the primary urgent screen
questions.explanation: Assess safety, functional impairment, psychosis and possible medical or substance-induced mimics.
questions.hint: Which features can require hospitalization?

questions.prompt: Why is a decreased need for sleep different from insomnia?
options: The patient feels rested despite little sleep rather than wanting sleep but being unable to obtain it
Both always mean the same physiology
Insomnia requires elevated energy by definition
questions.explanation: A reduced need for sleep is a classic mania symptom distinct from distressing inability to sleep.

questions.prompt: For severe acute mania, which broad treatment strategy is appropriate?
options: Antipsychotic and/or mood stabilizer with safety-focused care
Antidepressant monotherapy as first-line acute treatment
No treatment despite inability to care for self
questions.explanation: Acute mania treatment prioritizes safety, sleep restoration and mood stabilization; pharmacologic choices depend on context.
questions.hint: Choose therapy that reduces manic activation.

questions.prompt: What complication is a concern when patients have escalating impulsivity?
options: Financial loss, injury and dangerous behavior
questions.explanation: Mania may impair insight and decision-making, increasing high-stakes behavioral risks.

questions.prompt: Why is a careful longitudinal history needed before assigning bipolar I disorder?
options: Confirm an actual manic episode and rule out substances or medical causes
A single self-reported energetic hour establishes the diagnosis
Brain MRI always shows a diagnostic lesion
questions.explanation: Diagnosis depends on episode criteria, impairment and exclusions rather than a brief mood state.

stable: Sleep and behavior stabilize under a safe treatment plan.
unstable: The patient becomes more disorganized and unsafe, requiring evaluation for inpatient stabilization.

title: Fever after a medication change
scene: A 38-year-old taking several psychiatric medications has agitation, sweating, diarrhea and tremor after a new serotonergic agent was added.

questions.prompt: Which toxidrome best explains the symptoms?
questions.explanation: Recent serotonergic exposure with clonus, hyperreflexia and autonomic instability strongly suggests serotonin toxicity.
questions.hint: What neuromuscular finding distinguishes the syndrome?

questions.prompt: Which bedside finding most strongly supports the diagnosis over many alternatives?
options: Absent bowel sounds with dry skin
questions.explanation: Clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic neuromuscular findings in serotonin toxicity.
questions.hint: Look for increased rather than reduced reflexes.

questions.prompt: What is the underlying pharmacologic mechanism?
options: Excess central and peripheral serotonergic signaling
Direct loss of all dopamine in the substantia nigra
questions.explanation: Interactions or overdose can increase serotonergic activity, producing neuromuscular and autonomic excitation.
questions.hint: Think receptor-level excess rather than deficiency.

questions.prompt: What is the immediate management priority?
options: Stop serotonergic agents and provide supportive stabilization and cooling as indicated
questions.explanation: Stabilization, sedation when needed, temperature control and stopping offending agents are central; severe cases need intensive support.
questions.hint: Remove the offending driver and support organ function.

questions.prompt: Which complication can develop in a severe case?
questions.explanation: Severe muscle activity and hyperthermia can produce metabolic and end-organ injury.
questions.hint: What does sustained muscle activity do to muscle tissue?

questions.prompt: Which feature more often favors neuroleptic malignant syndrome instead?
options: Slower onset after dopamine blockade with marked rigidity
Prominent clonus within hours after a serotonergic combination
Diarrhea and hyperreflexia as the defining pair
Rapid resolution after a single oral antacid
questions.explanation: NMS often evolves over days and has marked rigidity and hyporeflexia or normal reflexes, whereas serotonin toxicity often appears rapidly with clonus/hyperreflexia.
questions.hint: Compare onset, medication mechanism and reflex findings.

stable: The offending drugs are withheld, and the patient improves with supportive management.
unstable: Temperature and rigidity worsen, prompting urgent intensive monitoring for organ injury.

title: Airway concerns before surgery
scene: A 56-year-old with limited neck extension, prior difficult intubation and severe obesity is scheduled for an urgent operation.
vitals: SpO₂ 96%; Mallampati IV; limited mouth opening

questions.prompt: What major perioperative risk should be planned for?
options: Difficult tracheal intubation and possible difficult ventilation
Acute appendicitis based on airway exam
questions.explanation: Multiple predictors and a prior difficult airway mandate a deliberate airway and rescue plan.
questions.hint: What procedure can be challenging given anatomy and history?

questions.prompt: Which planning step is most appropriate before induction?
options: Assess awake-airway options, oxygenation strategies, rescue devices and backup personnel
Induce anesthesia without a rescue plan
Avoid discussing the case with the team
questions.explanation: ASA guidance emphasizes preplanned primary and rescue strategies and awake intubation when indicated.
questions.hint: What is the strategy if unconscious airway control fails?

questions.prompt: Why does obesity often shorten safe apnea time?
options: Reduced functional residual capacity and increased oxygen consumption limit reserves
Obesity always increases functional residual capacity
The hemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve vanishes
questions.explanation: Reduced oxygen reserves and higher metabolic demand can lead to rapid desaturation during apnea.
questions.hint: Compare oxygen stores with oxygen use.

questions.prompt: When predicted difficult intubation is paired with difficult ventilation risk, what strategy may be favored?
options: Consider awake intubation while maintaining spontaneous ventilation
Always perform deep induction before any airway plan
questions.explanation: An awake technique may preserve spontaneous breathing and airway tone in selected high-risk patients.
questions.hint: Why maintain ventilation until the tube is secured?

questions.prompt: What is a dangerous response to repeated unsuccessful attempts?
options: Task fixation that delays oxygenation and rescue ventilation
questions.explanation: Repeated attempts can cause edema and injury while desaturation progresses; pivot to oxygenation and rescue algorithms.
questions.hint: Time, attempts and saturation all matter.

questions.prompt: Why is confirmation of effective ventilation more important than simply visualizing a tube passing the cords?
options: A tube may be misplaced or obstructed despite apparent placement
Pulse oximetry alone instantly proves tracheal location
questions.explanation: Use continuous waveform capnography and clinical assessment to confirm ventilation and tracheal placement.
questions.hint: What monitors exhaled CO₂?

stable: A planned, team-supported airway is secured with confirmation and backup available.
unstable: Ventilation becomes difficult after induction, requiring early rescue and oxygenation priority.

title: A sudden change in the operating room
scene: A previously healthy 19-year-old under general anesthesia develops unexplained rising end-tidal CO₂, tachycardia and muscle rigidity shortly after volatile anesthetic exposure.
vitals: ETCO₂ rising despite ventilation; HR 145; temperature climbing

questions.prompt: What emergency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Hypercarbia, rigidity and hypermetabolism after triggering anesthesia suggest malignant hyperthermia.
questions.hint: Think skeletal muscle calcium release and anesthetic triggers.

questions.prompt: Which early monitor change is particularly important?
options: Unexpected increase in end-tidal CO₂ despite increased minute ventilation
Sustained low end-tidal CO₂ as the mandatory initial sign
A single isolated low platelet count
questions.explanation: Rapid CO₂ production from hypermetabolism often precedes marked temperature elevation.
questions.hint: What metabolite rises first with excessive muscle metabolism?

questions.prompt: What cellular abnormality drives the crisis?
options: Uncontrolled sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release in skeletal muscle
Complete loss of acetylcholine release at every neuromuscular junction
Blockade of sodium reabsorption in the kidney
questions.explanation: Often linked to altered excitation–contraction coupling such as RYR1, excessive Ca²⁺ cycling consumes ATP and generates heat and CO₂.
questions.hint: Which intracellular ion activates skeletal muscle contraction?

questions.prompt: What is the immediate treatment priority?
options: Stop triggers, deliver 100% oxygen and administer dantrolene with full supportive management
Continue volatile anesthetic at higher concentration
questions.explanation: The crisis requires immediate trigger cessation, dantrolene, ventilation, cooling and metabolic/electrolyte management.
questions.hint: What drug reduces abnormal calcium release?

questions.prompt: Which metabolic complication is especially dangerous?
options: Hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis with dysrhythmia risk
questions.explanation: Muscle breakdown and acidemia can drive severe potassium shifts and end-organ injury.
questions.hint: What escapes damaged myocytes?

questions.prompt: Why must patients remain under observation after apparent initial control?
options: Recrudescence and delayed metabolic complications can occur
Dantrolene instantly eliminates all risk forever
The condition is never associated with renal injury
questions.explanation: Recurrence and rhabdomyolysis warrant ongoing monitoring and specialist consultation.
questions.hint: Consider recurrence and organ injury after crisis termination.

stable: Triggers are stopped and dantrolene is administered promptly with monitored recovery.
unstable: Hyperkalemia and severe acidosis develop, requiring urgent targeted metabolic management.

title: Hypotension after a regional technique

questions.prompt: Which mechanism most likely explains the early hypotension?

Total peripheral vasoconstriction from the spinal injection
questions.explanation: Neuraxial sympathetic blockade causes arterial and venous vasodilation, reducing preload and systemic vascular resistance.
questions.hint: Which autonomic outflow is blocked?

questions.prompt: What immediate monitoring focus is appropriate?
options: Frequent BP, HR, respiratory function and block level assessment
questions.explanation: Rapidly escalating blockade can impair hemodynamics and respiration.
questions.hint: Watch both circulation and breathing.

questions.prompt: Why can heart rate decrease as the block becomes higher?
options: Cardioaccelerator sympathetic fibers may be blocked and venous return reduced
A higher block always stimulates beta-1 receptors
Direct sinoatrial tissue necrosis is inevitable
The vagus nerve is surgically severed
questions.explanation: Block of upper thoracic sympathetics and reduced venous return may favor bradycardia.
questions.hint: Which spinal segments contribute to cardiac sympathetic tone?

questions.prompt: What is a reasonable immediate management framework?
options: Support oxygenation, position and intravascular volume appropriately, and give suitable vasopressors with escalation
questions.explanation: Hypotension from neuraxial blockade requires prompt hemodynamic support and assessment for a high spinal.
questions.hint: Restore perfusion, evaluate ventilation and raise help early.

questions.prompt: Which finding signals potentially life-threatening high neuraxial block?

questions.explanation: High or total spinal blockade can impair respiratory muscles and cardiovascular sympathetic support.

questions.prompt: Why is sedation escalation dangerous in a patient reporting dyspnea during a rising block?
options: Sedation may mask neurologic deterioration and worsen ventilation
questions.explanation: Evaluate airway, breathing and block progression before attributing symptoms to anxiety.
questions.hint: Protect the capacity to detect deterioration.

stable: Blood pressure normalizes and the block level stabilizes under close monitoring.
unstable: Upper extremity weakness and respiratory difficulty emerge, prompting immediate airway and cardiovascular rescue planning.

sources.label: NYSORA — High or Total Spinal Anesthesia
